title: Agenda: Matthew and Cyrus, Wednesday 2026-11-11, 10:00 Mountain
sub: The topics Matthew brings to his meeting with Cyrus on Wednesday 2026-11-11 at 10:00 Mountain time (MST, Boulder; the usual time), carrying over the work that continues from their meeting of 2026-11-05 (^report(37)), in two parts: performance (undo, and Hazel compiled to JS) and hazeljs for other JavaScript developers. A work in progress: updated as items move until the meeting, so each item says where it stands, as of when, and what it needs from the meeting.
short: Performance: undo's time is linear because of a few whole-program passes, not the history, and its space is nearly flat when compacted; hazel-jit will measure JS's best case on polygon-heavy views.
hazeljs for others: a README PR on dev points JS developers to the package, and a report will show how Dress Up scripts its rooms in Hazel.

sections.title: 1. Performance: undo, and Hazel compiled to JS
sections.intro: Two threads from the last meeting. Undo: what it costs as programs grow, and how close it can get to O(log n). And a new experiment decided there: compile livelits' view functions to JavaScript, to see how much faster Hazel code can get. Measured in Node on #2635 (livelits × modular editors) unless an item says otherwise.

items.title: Undo and redo in O(log n), in space and in time: how close are we, and why not yet?
items.status: measured; the O(log n) design is open
items.body:
Matthew showed Cyrus the analysis of undo's cost on 2026-11-05 (^report(38)). The two questions continue: how do we get closer to O(log n) for an undo and a redo, in space and in time, and why are we not there yet, in each.

Time, where it stands. Every step grows in proportion to the program: on a program of n top-level definitions, an edit, an undo and a redo each have a log-log slope of 1.1 to 1.16 (^report(36)). Three fixes on #2635 made each step cheaper without changing that: the program's root id read from a cache (394552d5d0), no completions after a numeral (bfa36a6ede), and realizing the view after an undo no longer counted as an edit (9df1b2601e). Now a redo costs about an edit (41 ms against 46 at 3,200 definitions, dev build, one run), and an undo costs an edit plus a rebuild of the outline (85 ms).

Time, why not O(log n) yet. The incremental caches do their part: an edit, an undo or a redo re-parses one or two definitions and re-measures one or two chunks. What is linear is a handful of passes around them that walk every top-level definition: MakeTerm's top-level pass (about 38% of the profile at 3,200 definitions), DefStatics' walk of the chain of definitions (20%), the outline rebuilt from scratch on an undo (15%; only #2469's modular editors have it) and Measured's walk (6%). None of it is the undo history: pushing and popping an entry costs almost nothing. The top level is a list of definitions, so any pass over it, or any summary of it rebuilt after a change, is O(n). Not measured yet: evaluation and the view during an undo.

Space, where it stands. Dev keeps a whole copy of the editor for every edit, and caps the history only when a setting that is off by default is on (on #2597, Full Body kept 89 MB more per edit). Andrew Blinn's compaction (6010128b7d, on #2469 and #2635) drops each entry's derived data and keeps its zippers: then an entry adds about 0.01 MB at 400, 1,600 and 6,400 definitions, flat, because consecutive entries share nearly all their structure (^ticket(665), GitHub run 41695584813).

Space, why not O(log n) yet. Two parts are still linear. The newest entry of each stack is kept whole so that the latest undo is fast (032fe3aca6): 0.55, 1.9 and 6.9 MB at the three sizes, about 1.1 KB a definition. And what compaction drops (syntax, statics, evaluation) is rebuilt on a restore, so the space saved is paid in time. One caveat on the flat number: the probe typed into the same definition again and again; edits spread over the program may share less.

Toward O(log n), the candidates. (a) The top level as a balanced tree of definitions, each node with summaries of its subtree (the names it binds, its part of the skeleton, its rows): each pass touches only the edited definition's path, an entry shares every other node, and the worker's request after an edit shrinks the same way (^ticket(666) found a one-literal edit re-sends about 10% of a chain of lets, every let around the edit hashing anew). (b) Undo as an inverse edit applied to the live state, so derived data updates as it does for a keystroke and no snapshot needs rebuilding. (c) First, and cheapest: build the outline incrementally, which every undo pays for, and every edit while the sidebar is shown.
items.meeting: Cyrus's read of the two directions, a balanced tree of definitions or undo as an inverse edit, and which to prototype first. Is the incremental outline the right first step? For space: does flat-per-compacted-entry answer the question, or should the next measurement spread edits over the program, use a release build, or count the newest whole entry differently?

items.title: hazel-jit: livelit views compiled to JS, to see the best case
items.status: views run compiled in the app: a Polygons render 13.0 ms on the interpreter, 0.83 ms compiled
items.body:
Update, 11-06 16:15: the work has its own report, report 045 (hazel-jit: Livelit Views Compiled to JavaScript, work in progress). Slice 3 (7a7151443c) carries the model into JS and the answer back, an event handler coming back as a Hazel function, and runs views compiled in the app (eval_view, the setting Compiled views, on by default, the interpreter when it cannot). A Polygons render: 13.0 ms on the interpreter, 0.83 ms compiled, of which 0.05 ms is the compiled call: the trip in and out is now most of the cost. What follows is the item as first written.

Started 2026-11-06, on a trial branch off #2635 (trial/694-view-jit, 79fe5bbebf). HazelJit.compile turns an elaborated term into a JS function, modules included. The Polygons slide's livelit compiles whole (no member left out, 24 KB of JS), and its view, applied to the model the slide's own shirt gives it, returns the same view command as the interpreter, its whole Html tree; 26 smaller programs agree too, the Petri net rule of ^report(43) among them. Breaking the compiler on purpose fails the tests, so the comparison is real. First numbers (Node, a dev build, medians of 30, two runs): the view's program takes 12 to 17 ms on the interpreter and 0.06 to 0.09 ms compiled, 140 to 300 times faster, after 2 ms to compile. Not counted yet: carrying the model into JS and the command tree back, and the call memo the app uses. Next: that boundary (an event handler in the Html has to come back as a Hazel function), the setting, and timings in browsers.

The idea, in Matthew's words (2026-11-06): Reason code, called hazel-jit, that compiles some of a Hazel program's syntax tree into JavaScript that does mostly the same thing, and calls that instead of the interpreter. Messed Up Dress Up already has three kinds of handler for the same rule: the game's own JS, a Hazel function and a Fumola one, each written by hand. hazel-jit would be a general way to replace slow Hazel subroutines with JS made from them.

The best case first. Numbers need not match exactly for now: overflow, rounding and the like may differ between Hazel's numbers and JS's. The question is how much faster JS could make some Hazel subroutines at best.

What to compile first: the livelit view functions on the slides, especially those that draw many user-defined polygons. In the Livelit Playground deck: Polygons and Polygon Viewer, then Full Body (2,929 lines, the most polygons), the Witch, Hands, and the Scenes slide's woods.

The design so far (^ticket(694), 2026-11-05): hazel-jit turns an elaborated term into JS source and runs it with new Function. It covers variables, functions and recursive functions with their closures, application, let, match and its patterns, if, tuples and labels, lists (as cons cells, so :: stays constant time), literals, operators, constructors, and builtins (JS versions of the common ones, the rest through a bridge to the OCaml builtin). Types, ascriptions and parentheses are erased. Anything else (holes, tests, filters, projectors, splices) leaves the view on the interpreter, with the reason kept. Only a view and what its closure reaches are compiled, not update, init, expand or the program. The model goes in as JS and the command tree comes back as a Hazel value, so the drawing is unchanged. A setting, jit_views, on by default. Lost while compiled: the call memo's sharing between renders, probes inside the view, and the step budget.

Timings: for each slide, the interpreter's time, the compile time, and the compiled view's time with the boundary crossing, as medians with ranges, in Node first, then in browsers on GitHub's machines.
items.meeting: Is the best-case framing right, numbers allowed to differ? Is compiling the view alone the right first cut? What would make a convincing comparison: which slides, and against what (the interpreter with its call memo, or the game's hand-written JS)?

items.title: BuckleScript and ReScript (and Melange): to know, and to compare with
items.body:
Cyrus named BuckleScript and ReScript as technologies to know about, and perhaps compare with, if not use. What they are, briefly, to be checked as part of ^ticket(698): BuckleScript, from Bloomberg (2016), compiled OCaml to readable JavaScript. Its team later renamed it ReScript, with a syntax of its own, aimed at the JavaScript world (version 12 in 2026). Melange is a fork that kept OCaml and Reason syntax, with first-class support in dune. Hazel itself is compiled to JS by js_of_ocaml, which works from OCaml's bytecode: a different route.

Three ways they bear on hazel-jit: (1) a reference for its output, since they map a typed functional language's values to JS (variants, records, lists, closures, functions of several arguments) and are known for fast, readable output; (2) a route to use: turn Hazel into OCaml, Reason or ReScript and let their compiler make the JS, ahead of time, or in the page if their compiler runs there; (3) Hazel's own build: what Melange's output would do to the speed of Hazel's evaluator, against js_of_ocaml's, a larger question.
items.meeting: Which did Cyrus have in mind: a reference for hazel-jit's output, a tool to use, or a different compiler for Hazel itself?

sections.title: 2. hazeljs for other JavaScript developers
sections.intro: hazeljs is Hazel as a JavaScript library, on npm since 2026-11-02, and Messed Up Dress Up is the first program to use it for its scripts (a Hazlet: a JS program whose event handlers are written in Hazel). The next step is people outside the project: first, the group in Cambridge Cyrus mentioned, who simulate Petri nets with JS tools of their own.

items.title: A PR to dev: Hazel's README links to the experimental hazeljs package
items.body:
Opened 2026-11-06: #2812 (branch docs/readme-hazeljs, README only; CI running). A small PR against dev: a short section in Hazel's README on hazeljs, the experimental npm package (source: hazelgrove/hazeljs; 0.0.4 is the latest): Hazel as a JavaScript library, to analyze and run Hazel programs from Node or a web page and call the functions they define. It notes that the plan is for the package to track dev, but that it does not yet: it is built from the draft library in #2711 and #2719 (at 1ba138ef28). At the last meeting, hazeljs following dev was settled as the direction, perhaps after #2469 lands, and not urgent.

Why now: Cyrus knows people in Cambridge who simulate Petri nets with JavaScript tools of their own. Matthew would like to see whether they could move some of their JS logic into Hazel through hazeljs, to gain Hazel's types and its clarity in the middle of an edit. A link from Hazel's own README gives them a place to start.
items.meeting: Who should review it? And Cyrus's contacts in Cambridge: who they are, and whether he will introduce them.

items.title: A report for JS developers: scripting your app in Hazel, the way MUDU does
items.status: drafted: ^report(43) live, ^report(44), and an example repository
items.body:
Since 2026-11-06 afternoon: ^report(43)'s example runs on its page, every Hazel listing in Hazel's own editor with go to definition between listings, and an event log as the game's; ^report(44) says how any article can have such listings; and the example is an app of its own, in a public repository, matthewhammer/hazeljs-petri-example (0.0.1; its site, in the game's style, is planned). hazeljs's README now has both apps under Examples, with links to the two reports. Building it found a bug in hazeljs: a JS object whose keys come in another order than its type's fields gets stuck when a field is a list.

Drafted 2026-11-06: ^report(43), Scripting a JavaScript App in Hazel (work in progress). It explains the pattern and the game's pieces, with links to their lines in the game's code, then six steps for another app, then a worked Petri net example (two processes and a lock; the firing rule in two Hazel modules), run in Node through hazeljs 0.0.4. Its findings: the rule ran as written; in 2,000 random steps the two processes were never both busy; a mistake in a rule is reported by module before anything runs, while the app's own JS answers; a call costs about 3.5 ms against 0.7 µs for the same handler in JS, and a build 340 to 440 ms. That is fine for each click, but not for a simulator's inner loop, which ties this item to hazel-jit (item 2).

A Hazel report on how Messed Up Dress Up uses hazeljs for its scripts, written for another JavaScript developer who wants to do the same in their own program. It builds on ^report(33) (the game's scripts), ^report(34) (a library for Hazel in JS) and ^report(39) (Hazlets so far), but speaks to someone outside the project.

What it would cover: (1) the shape: the app hands an event and a typed view of its state to a Hazel function, and acts out the command it returns; Hazel never touches the page. (2) How the game does it: each room's on_event : (Globals, Event) -> Cmd, a program of modules (Common, then one per room) built by Hazel.runProgram, errors and holes reported module by module, the game's own JS answering while the program is unfinished, and the event log. (3) The steps for your app: install, write the types, call the function per event, interpret the commands. (4) Costs and limits today: a Hazel rule answers in about 3.5 ms of a 13.7 ms lever pull, the first event after a reset waits 0.5 to 0.7 s, and the package is a 0.0.x prototype. (5) A small worked example in another domain, perhaps a Petri net's firing rule, for the readers in Cambridge.
